title: Why getting up is so hard with ADHD
hook: For many people with ADHD, the alarm rings in the middle of their inner night. Three causes, and what moves the clock.

lines.text: You asked why getting up is so hard with ADHD. The short answer: for many, the alarm rings in the middle of their night.
It is not weak will. Three things pile up: a body clock that runs late, a brain that starts up slowly, and a start that offers no reward.
Yesterday’s episode touched on the body clock. Today we look at the whole morning, step by step, and at what helps.

</g>

lines.text: Sleep is controlled by two forces. The first is sleep pressure. It builds up every hour you are awake, like sand in an hourglass.
The second is the body clock. It opens a window for sleep at night, announced by the hormone melatonin.
You fall asleep easily only when both agree: enough pressure, and an open window.
And waking up is easy only when the pressure is used up, and the clock has switched to day.

lines.text: With ADHD, the clock is the problem. In about three out of four people with ADHD, the whole rhythm is delayed.
Melatonin rises about one and a half hours later than usual. So the sleep window opens later, and it also closes later.
This is not a habit that crept in. It shows up in hormone measurements, and already in children.
It means: at eleven at night, the window is still shut. Going to bed on time only produces lying awake.

lines.text: Then the evening adds its own pull. At night, nobody wants anything from you. No messages, no demands.
For a brain that fights distraction all day, this is the hour when it finally works well. Many people with ADHD feel most awake after ten.
Screens make it worse. In one experiment, reading on a tablet before bed pushed the body clock back by more than an hour, compared with a printed book.
And stopping something interesting in order to do something boring, like going to bed, is the exact task this brain is worst at.

</g>

lines.text: Now do the arithmetic. The window opens at one in the morning. The alarm is set for half past six.
That is five and a half hours, night after night. Most adults need seven to eight.
On the weekend, the body takes back what it can, and sleeps until eleven. That feels like recovery. But it tells the clock: morning starts late.
Researchers call the gap between body clock and alarm clock social jetlag. It is like flying two time zones west every Friday, and back every Monday.

quiz.q: On holiday, Mara sleeps from 1:00 to 9:00 and feels fine. On workdays she is in bed at 23:00, lies awake until 1:00, and suffers at 6:30. What fits both?

options.text: Stress on workdays keeps her awake and makes mornings hard
options.why: Stress can do that. But it would not explain why she lands on exactly the same hour, one o’clock, when she is free and relaxed.

options.text: Her evening habits are poor, so she cannot switch off
options.why: Being in bed at 23:00 is disciplined. And on holiday she falls asleep at 1:00 without trouble. Habits do not explain the fixed hour.

options.text: She needs more sleep than other people do
options.why: On holiday, eight hours are enough for her. The problem on workdays is when she can sleep, not how much she needs.

options.text: Her sleep window sits late, and an early bedtime does not move it
options.why: Free of duties, she drifts to one o’clock. Forced to bed earlier, she still falls asleep at one. The window stays put, only the alarm changes.

quiz.explain: Think of a shop with fixed opening hours, from one to nine. You can stand at the door at eleven, but it will not open earlier because you are there. That is Mara in bed at 23:00: the waiting is real, but the door stays shut. On holiday she simply arrives when the shop opens and stays until it closes, so everything feels easy. On workdays she has to leave at half past six, long before closing time. The amount of sleep she needs is ordinary. Her habits are fine. What differs from other people is the position of the opening hours, and going to bed earlier does not move them.

scenes.title: What the alarm really hits
scenes.svg:
<g data-l="0" data-fx="up"><circle cx="107" cy="110" r="52" class="fp si"/><path d="M107 110 L99.8 137.0" class="fn si s3"/><path d="M107 110 L107.0 152.0" class="fn si"/><circle cx="107" cy="110" r="4" class="fi"/><text x="107" y="190" class="mid tm tb fi">6:30</text><text x="107" y="210" class="mid ts fm">the wall clock</text></g>

<g ><line x1="170" y1="110" x2="220" y2="110" class="sb"/><polygon points="230,110 220,115.5 220,104.5" class="fb"/></g>
<text x="200" y="96" class="mid ts fb tb">−1.5 h</text>
</g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="238" width="352" height="64" rx="14" class="fp"/>
<path d="M62 258 a12 12 0 1 0 6 20.4 a9.36 9.36 0 1 1 -6 -20.4 z" class="fb"/>
<text x="84" y="264" class="ts">body temperature near its lowest</text>
<text x="84" y="286" class="ts">melatonin still in the blood</text>
</g>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="322" width="352" height="42" rx="12" class="fp"/>
<text x="200" y="349" class="mid tm">woken at five every day, and called lazy</text>
</g>

lines.text: So what does the alarm hit at half past six? For a typical body clock, half past six is the edge of morning.
For a clock that runs one and a half hours late, the same alarm lands at an inner time of five o’clock.
Body temperature is near its lowest point then, and melatonin is still in the blood. Every signal in the body says: night.
Imagine being woken at five every single day, and being called lazy for struggling. That is the situation.

quiz.q: Jonas’s melatonin rises at 0:30. The usual time is 22:00. His alarm rings at 7:00. Which inner time does it hit, compared with a typical clock?

options.why: That would be true for a clock without any delay. His melatonin shows a clear shift, so his inner time is earlier.
That adds the delay instead of subtracting it. A late clock means the body is behind the wall clock, not ahead of it.
His clock runs two and a half hours late: from 22:00 to 0:30. Seven o’clock minus two and a half hours is half past four.
That uses the one and a half hours from the example. But his own delay, from 22:00 to 0:30, is two and a half hours.

quiz.explain: Treat it like a time zone. Jonas’s body lives two and a half hours west of the place where he actually is. You get that number from the melatonin: it rises at half past midnight instead of at ten, and the difference is two and a half hours. When it is seven on the wall, it is therefore half past four in his body. The direction matters. A body that is behind has an earlier time than the wall clock, so you subtract. And the size matters too: the one and a half hours in the episode were an average. Each person has their own delay.

<text x="130" y="286" class="mid ts fc tb">front: last</text>
<text x="130" y="304" class="mid ts fm">planning, self-control</text>
</g>
<text x="200" y="334" class="mid ts" data-l="2" data-fx="up">thicker after a short night, and in the inner night</text>
<text x="200" y="364" class="mid ts fb tb" data-l="3" data-fx="up">with ADHD: both, almost every morning</text>

lines.text: Then comes the second problem: sleep inertia. It is the fog in the first minutes after waking.
The brain does not switch on all at once. The regions for planning and self-control, at the front, come back last.
Usually the fog lifts within half an hour. But it is much thicker after a short night, and when you wake during your inner night.
With ADHD, both conditions are met almost every morning. And the part that comes back last is the part that was weaker to begin with: the management.

lines.text: The third problem is the start itself. Remember the first ADHD episode: starting needs a signal that says, this is worth it.
Now look at the choice at half past six. A warm bed, right now. Against a benefit that lies hours away.
For a brain that discounts later rewards steeply, this is the most one-sided decision of the day. And it has to be made in the fog.
The snooze button is the logical result. It is a small reward now, bought with a slightly bigger problem later.

<text x="200" y="342" class="mid ts fm" data-l="3" data-fx="up">not proven, but better sleep often eases symptoms</text>

lines.text: Short sleep then feeds back into the day. Lack of sleep weakens attention and impulse control in everyone.
With ADHD, it weakens what was already weak. So a bad night makes the symptoms stronger, and stronger symptoms make the next evening later.
Some researchers go further. They see restlessness partly as a tired brain keeping itself awake, the way an overtired child gets wild instead of sleepy.
That idea is not proven. But it fits an old observation: when sleep improves, ADHD symptoms often ease a little.

lines.text: Two more things belong on the list, because they are more common with ADHD and easy to miss.
One is restless legs: an urge to move the legs in the evening that keeps you from falling asleep. In a large study, almost three in ten adults with ADHD reported such symptoms.
The other is the timing of medication. A stimulant taken too late in the day can push sleep even further back.
And if you are extremely sleepy during the day despite enough hours in bed, that is a reason to see a doctor.

lines.text: Now to what helps. The body clock can be moved, and its strongest signal is light.
Bright light in the morning shifts the clock earlier. Daylight outside is by far the strongest source, even under clouds.
In a small study, adults with ADHD used a bright lamp every morning for three weeks. Their rhythm moved earlier, and their symptoms improved.
There was no comparison group, though. So treat it as a hint, not as proof.
The evening is the mirror image. Dim light and no bright screen in the last hour keep the clock from sliding later.

lines.text: The second lever is melatonin itself. A Dutch trial tested it in 51 adults with ADHD and a delayed rhythm.
A very small dose, taken in the evening for three weeks, moved the inner evening about one and a half hours earlier. A dummy pill did nothing.
With an added morning lamp, the shift was almost two hours. ADHD symptoms dropped by 14 percent, but only in the group without the lamp.
And two weeks after the trial, everything was back where it started. Actual sleep times had barely moved.
So the clock can be shifted, but only as long as you keep at it, and only if your bedtime moves with it. Dose and timing are a matter for a doctor.

quiz.q: In the trial, melatonin plus lamp shifted the clock most, but only melatonin alone eased symptoms, and real sleep times barely moved. What follows?

options.text: The morning lamp cancels out the benefit of melatonin
options.why: Tempting, since only the lamp differs. But with about 17 people per group, one odd result may be chance. It needs a repeat first.

options.text: The clock can be shifted; that this eases symptoms is not shown
options.why: Shift and relief did not go together across the groups, and sleep itself did not change. The trial supports the first step and leaves the second one open.

options.text: The further the clock is shifted, the more the symptoms improve
options.why: The group with the biggest shift showed no improvement at all. The trial speaks against this simple rule.

options.text: Melatonin does not work, since everything returned to the start
options.why: A return after stopping shows that the effect needs continued use. It does not show that there was no effect while it was taken.

quiz.explain: Imagine three groups of people who want to lose weight. One group does nothing. One eats less, loses two kilos and feels fitter. One eats less and also runs, loses three kilos, but does not feel fitter. Would you conclude that running destroys fitness? Or that weight has nothing to do with it? With small groups, the honest answer is: weight clearly can be changed, and whether that is what makes people feel fitter needs a bigger study. The melatonin trial has exactly this shape. A hormone measurement moved in both treated groups. The outcome people care about moved in one of them, and the daily sleep times in neither.

lines.text: The third lever: hold the rhythm. The clock needs the same signal every day.
The most important fixed point is not the bedtime. It is the time you get up, including on weekends.
One hour later on Saturday is fine. Four hours later undoes a week of work.
That is hard, because the weekend sleep feels so deserved. A short nap after lunch is the better way to pay back sleep debt.

quiz.q: Which weekend plan protects Monday morning best for someone with a delayed body clock?

options.text: Stay in a darkened room on Sunday morning, to rest properly
options.why: Rest sounds right. But morning light is the signal that moves the clock earlier. A dark morning removes the one thing that helps.

options.text: Go to bed at 21:00 on Sunday, to be well rested on Monday
options.why: Sensible with a normal clock. With a delayed one, the sleep window is still shut at 21:00, so it mostly produces hours of lying awake.

options.text: Get up at most an hour later than usual, and go into daylight soon after
options.why: It keeps the fixed point almost in place and adds the strongest signal for an earlier clock. Lost sleep can be repaid with a short nap.

options.text: Sleep until noon on both days, to pay back the sleep debt in full
options.why: It does repay sleep. But two late mornings tell the clock that the day starts at noon, and Monday’s alarm lands even deeper in the inner night.

quiz.explain: Picture the body clock as a dog that pulls on the lead toward a later time, a little every day. Each morning with light and a fixed time to get up is a tug back. A weekend of sleeping until noon lets go of the lead for two days, and on Monday you start from further away than on Friday. An early bedtime does not help, because the dog cannot be pushed from behind: sleep only comes when the window opens. So the plan that works keeps the morning signal alive on Saturday and Sunday, with a small allowance, and repays the missing sleep at a time that does not move the clock.

lines.text: And finally, the first ten minutes. Do not rely on a decision made in the fog. Decide the evening before, and let things do the work.
A light alarm that brightens the room before the sound. And the alarm itself out of reach, so that you have to stand up.
A reward that waits: coffee on a timer, or a favourite podcast that is only allowed in the morning.
And a first step so small that it needs no willpower: feet on the floor. The clothes are already laid out, so nothing has to be chosen.

lines.text: The short version. With ADHD, the alarm often rings during the inner night. The brain starts up slowly, and the start offers no reward.
So do not fight the morning with willpower. Move the clock with morning light and a fixed time to get up.
Protect the evening from bright screens, and build the first ten minutes outside your head.
Thank you for the question. If you have another one, write it into the feedback field.

takeaways: In about three of four people with ADHD, the body clock runs late: melatonin rises about 1.5 hours later, so the sleep window opens and closes later.
An early alarm then hits the inner night. Going to bed earlier does not move the window, it mostly produces lying awake.
Sleep inertia is thicker after short nights and in the inner night, and the brain regions for planning come back last.
Getting up is a start with no immediate reward, decided in the fog. Short sleep then worsens attention the next day.
The clock can be moved: bright light in the morning, dim light in the evening, and a fixed time to get up, also on weekends.
Low-dose melatonin shifted the clock in a trial, but only while it was taken, and without moving real sleep times. Dose and timing belong with a doctor.
